newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. mediation faces chasm of Mideast mistrust.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mediation faces chasm of Mideast mistrust.

text.p: U.S. efforts to resolve a crisis in Israeli-Palestinian ties will have to bridge a chasm of mistrust between the two sides after months of deadlock and a double suicide bomb attack in Jerusalem.
Analysts say that for Washington's Middle East envoy Dennis Ross, expected to visit the region later this week, just getting Palestinians and Israelis into face-to-face talks will be tough.

The spiral of recriminations over last Wednesday's attack, in which two human bombs killed 13 other people in a packed Jerusalem market, follows a long standoff since Israel started building a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem in March.
"It's very hard to make expectations from Ross's visit," said Ghassan al-Khatib, a former Palestinian negotiator.
"I don't think he will come with concrete proposals...just an attempt to resume contacts."
U.S. officials have said Ross may come to Israel around the end of the week, after a seven-day period of mourning for the victims of the Jerusalem market attack.
Neither Israelis nor Palestinians expect him to engineer a dramatic breakthrough.

"It's premature to tell...There is an almost total breakdown in relations," chief Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat said when asked if Ross could get Palestinians and Israelis to sit down together for talks.
Each side accuses the other of violating central issues in their interim accords on Palestinian self-rule since 1993.

Israel's right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who inherited the accords from previous Labour governments, says Palestinian President Yasser Arafat has done "damn all" to meet commitments to halt violence against Israelis.

Palestinians say Israel's settlement-building on land they claim for a future state strikes at the heart of the 1993 accord. They also condemn Israel's closure of Palestinian territories after the bombings as collective punishment.

"The emphasis will not be on solving things, just getting them to talk," said Professor Barry Rubin of the Begin-Sadat Centre for Strategic Studies. "Dennis Ross wants to see what the two sides are saying. He's not going to succeed in a few days."
Israel insists that Ross concentrate on reviving Palestinian security cooperation with the Jewish state.

"We expect Ross to focus on the security issue. This is the only way the peace process can be salvaged," Netanyahu's communications adviser David Bar-Illan told Reuters. "I don't want to be pessimistic. I'm hoping the Palestinian Authority is as interested as we are in saving the peace," he said.
But he said Israel would not be convinced overnight that its demands for greater Palestinian security efforts were being met.
"It would take time. So far not a single step has been taken," he said.
Palestinians say Ross must address wider concerns on his visit, primarily Israel's settlement policy.

"We need a major initiative that is balanced," Erekat said. "The situation is deteriorating hour by hour and Ross must deal with the substance of the reasons which led to the crisis in the peace process."
"It all depends what it is in Ross's suitcase," he added.
Khatib said Ross was unlikely to steer the two sides away from further confrontations.
"I think he will be able to say they resumed contacts. They will ensure the resumption of the talks and then leave them to move onto the next crisis," he said.

Talks between the two sides have been stalled since March when Israel broke ground for a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem on a hill known as Jabal Abu Ghneim to Palestinians and Har Homa to Israelis.
Last week's double suicide bombing was the worst violence since Netanyahu took office in June last year. Islamic militants killed 57 people in a wave of suicide bombings earlier in 1996.
